blocks.text: Millions of organic compounds occur in nature and many thousands of new ones are made every year, so IUPAC (the International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry) set rules for naming them systematically from their structures. A systematic name is based on the parent hydrocarbon and has these parts:

items: Stem or root: the longest continuous carbon chain that includes the carbon bearing the functional group; that carbon gets the lowest possible number. A ring adds the prefix cyclo.
Primary suffix (suffix of the stem): shows whether the chain is saturated or unsaturated: -an-, -en- or -yn-.
Secondary suffix (suffix of the functional group): gives the family name, e.g. -ol, -al, -one.

Prefix: the name and position of any side chain (alkyl group) or substituent, such as halo or nitro, with the number of the carbon it is attached to. Without a prefix the name is just stem plus suffixes.

blocks.alt: Four coloured boxes name the parts of a systematic name: prefix, stem, primary suffix and secondary suffix. Two worked examples: Cl-CH2-CH2-CH2-CHO, numbered from the CHO carbon, is 4-chloro + but + an + al = 4-chlorobutanal; CH3-C(CH3)=CH-CH2-OH, numbered from the CH2OH end, is 3-methyl + but + 2-en + 1-ol = 3-methylbut-2-en-1-ol.
blocks.caption: The parts of a systematic name, with two worked examples (original diagram after the book's scheme).
blocks.long_description: Read a systematic name from left to right as prefix, stem, primary suffix and secondary suffix. In the first example the chain has four carbons (but), only single bonds (an) and an aldehyde group (al), with a chlorine on carbon 4. In the second the four-carbon chain has a double bond starting at carbon 2 (2-en), an OH group on carbon 1 (1-ol) and a methyl group on carbon 3.

blocks.title: A slip in the book's first example
blocks.text: The book numbers the chain of Cl-CH2-CH2-CH2-CHO from 1 to 4 but splits its name as '4-chloro prop an al'. A four-carbon chain has the stem but-, so the name is 4-chlorobutanal.
